work.html.text: Skip to content Selected work Media · Product · AI · Operations NARRATIVE MECHANICS Work Writing AI & Media About Work Selected things I've helped build, scale, or operate. Two cases that show how media, product, marketing, content, audience relationships, and operations have to work together when a format or company is still taking shape. Posta Podcast company · Buenos Aires and Latin America Posta began in 2014, before podcasting was an obvious media category in the region. The work was not only making shows. It was building the product, explaining the format to audiences and brands, developing repeat listening and community relationships, creating repeatable production and distribution, and turning an editorial idea into an operating company. Context A format before its market On-demand audio had promise, but limited shared language, established commercial models, or regional production infrastructure. Role Co-founder Product, marketing, growth, positioning, and business development across the company's development. What changed From experiment to regional company Posta built an original catalog, branded audio work, and operations beyond Argentina. PodX acquired a majority stake in 2022. Read the Posta case study Roxom TV 24/7 global live media · San Francisco, London, Hong Kong Roxom TV posed a different problem: how to run a live global media product continuously without copying the cost structure and organizational shape of a traditional television network. Context Continuous output across time zones Live production, editorial work, real-time data, programming, and recovery paths had to behave like one system. Role Founding team Media architecture and product operations, including workflows, internal tools, automation, and remote operational work. What changed A distributed operating model Studios across three continents connected to shared product, editorial, production, and AI-assisted workflows. Read the Roxom TV case study The thread between them. Posta and Roxom TV look like different kinds of media company. The underlying work was similar: connect product, marketing, content, audience, and operations so a shift in distribution or production becomes a system people can run every day. That foundation now runs through my work on AI-native media : how research, interfaces, workflows, editorial operations, distribution, communities, and decision-making change when AI becomes part of the infrastructure. For more examples of what I am building, see the public product shelf . For the ideas behind the work, start with Writing . Bring a concrete problem. A new format, a production workflow that keeps breaking, or a product people struggle to understand: these are useful starting points. I look at the audience, the editorial decisions, the tools, and who has to run the work every day. Tell me what you are building, what is getting stuck, and what needs to change. The cases above show the kind of work I bring to that conversation. ai-media.html.text: Skip to content AI-Native Media Media · Product · Marketing · Content · Communities · AI NARRATIVE MECHANICS Work Writing AI & Media About Living topic hub AI-Native Media My work with AI-native media starts from earlier experience in media, products, marketing, content, audiences, and communities. The question is not how to add generated content, but what changes when AI becomes part of the operating system. The foundation comes first. AI is a new layer in a longer system. Media still needs a product people can use, marketing and distribution that make it discoverable, content with editorial purpose, and relationships that turn an audience into something more durable. Digital media Formats need companies and operating systems around them Posta and Roxom TV show two different transitions: on-demand audio and continuous global live media. Digital products The public surface and internal machinery are one product system Interfaces, workflows, tools, feedback loops, and recovery paths determine whether an idea can work repeatedly. Marketing and distribution Strong work still fails when people or systems cannot find and classify it Positioning, channels, packaging, metadata, and mediated discovery shape what reaches fair consideration. Content and editorial strategy Programming and judgment need an operable workflow Research, preparation, production, publishing, and accountability belong to the same editorial system. Audiences and communities Reach, return, participation, and belonging are different outcomes Automation can scale output and distribution; it cannot by itself create trust, shared language, or community. What I mean by AI-native media. AI-native media is not traditional media plus generated content. It begins when machine capabilities and constraints shape the product and operation from the start. That does not mean every step becomes automated. It means deciding deliberately where machines can carry bounded work, where they can improve an interface, where they introduce new failure modes, and where human judgment remains the system's point of accountability. Workflow Research, preparation, metadata, and repetitive execution AI can compress setup work and carry well-defined steps, provided the inputs, outputs, owners, and escalation paths are clear. Product Interfaces that understand context and intent The product can help people navigate complexity, not only generate more material for them to process. Operations State, automation, monitoring, and recovery The useful system is observable under pressure and gives a person a clear path back when automation fails. Discovery Content interpreted by machines before people Metadata, entity clarity, citations, provenance, and structure become part of editorial distribution. Start with one workflow. Pick a task that takes too much preparation or breaks at a handoff. Map its inputs, editorial decisions, owner, and failure cases before deciding what to automate. The useful result is a workflow someone can inspect and recover, with a clear reason for each automated step. My Roxom TV case study provides operating context. Before You Delegate examines the decisions that need to stay explicit. If you are working through a similar problem, tell me about the workflow . Agents are infrastructure, not characters. I evaluate agents by the work they can complete, the limits on their actions, and how they report problems. A useful agent needs a defined job, access to the relevant information, a record of its actions, and a way to ask for help. In a media workflow, that might mean preparing research packets, checking metadata, watching operational state, assembling a draft rundown, or moving approved material through distribution. The design question is not “What can the agent do?” It is “What can the system safely let the agent do, how will we know what happened, and who owns the result?” Humans, algorithms, and agents. Media now communicates with at least three kinds of audience. They overlap, but they do not read in the same way. Humans People looking for meaning, usefulness, or experience They need clear ideas, evidence, voice, context, and a reason to trust the source. Algorithms Distribution systems deciding what becomes visible They classify, rank, recommend, suppress, and repackage content according to incentives the publisher does not control. Agents Systems acting on a person's behalf They retrieve, compare, summarize, cite, and sometimes act. They need stable entities, explicit relationships, clean structure, and defensible sources. Writing for all three does not mean keyword stuffing or flattening every idea into machine prose. It means making the source and structure clear enough that mediation does not erase the meaning. Things I've learned building these systems. Roxom TV Continuous media turns every small ambiguity into an operational cost Handoffs, state, observability, recovery, and interface design are editorial infrastructure. Posta Format shifts change discovery and business models before incumbents notice Cheaper production matters, but the distribution interface often determines what can become durable. Agents Boundaries create leverage An agent becomes more useful when its authority, inputs, outputs, and failure paths become less ambiguous. Human role Accountability does not disappear when execution is delegated Editorial judgment, operational ownership, and recovery remain human responsibilities even when machines carry more steps. Writing. March 10, 2026 Origin Gravity Why an encounter with someone’s work can lead a reader to seek its source and keep reading. March 10, 2026 The Empty Room What a request, click, or reply tells us about an audience when some of the activity is automated. March 10, 2026 The Proxy Self A public profile can keep repeating a position after its author has moved on. What happens to the relationship? March 10, 2026 The Trust Collapse What readers assume about the person behind a byline, post, or reply, and why the production process matters. March 10, 2026 Writing for the Filter What changes when a platform selects an essay and an assistant summarizes it before a person reads it. March 7, 2026 Already Decided I built systems that act before I check in. A personal account of delegated decisions and the work that remains mine. Full index All writing Essays, frameworks, notes, and current lines of thought. Projects, nuggets, and speaking. Public products provide inspectable evidence for these ideas. They connect claims about agents, editorial systems, audience interaction, automation, and product strategy to things that can be opened and used. writing-for-the-filter.html.text: Skip to content Buenos Aires · Since 2008 Essays · Frameworks · Guided reading paths · About the author NARRATIVE MECHANICS Work Writing AI & Media About After You Post · 03 · March 2026 Writing forthe Filter Published March 10, 2026 · Updated September 14, 2026 · by Diego Dell'Agostino On content that has to pass two algorithmic layers before reaching a human, and why that changes what good editorial strategy is. Diego Dell'Agostino · Buenos Aires FILTER 01 FILTER 02 TWO MACHINES before the human There used to be one machine between you and a human reader. You learned to write for it. That was the job. Now there are two. The first decides whether to surface your content. The second, sitting between the first and the actual person, decides whether to read it. They have different criteria. The second filter changes what the first filter’s metrics can tell you. Section 01 The Second Filter There used to be one filter between your content and a human reader: the algorithm that decided whether to surface it. SEO was the science of surviving that filter. Understand what the algorithm rewarded, produce that, get shown. The optimization loop was legible: write for the machine so the machine shows you to the person. That loop still exists. But there's a second filter now sitting between the first one and the human, and it doesn't work the same way. The first filter decides what to surface. The second filter, the agent browsing on someone's behalf, decides what to read, what to summarize, what to pass along, and what to discard. Two machines in sequence before a person sees anything. I think the two filters create different pressures: earning attention and surviving compression. That is a way of looking at the problem, not a description of every ranking system. A hook may bring someone to a piece without helping a summary carry its argument. If the claim, evidence, and conclusion are hard to find, there is more room for the intermediary to lose the point. You spent years learning to write for a machine that showed you to people. Now there's another machine that reads you instead of them. And the human using that agent doesn't know what was omitted. They got an answer. The gap between your piece and their understanding is invisible to everyone. Section 02 The User Who Doesn't Know The human who uses a search engine today is often running their query through an agent without knowing it. Google now answers many questions directly at the top of the page, before any links. An assistant can assemble an answer with source links that the person may never open. These aren't power users with autonomous setups. They're ordinary people doing ordinary searches, and an intermediary is reading on their behalf before the results arrive. An answer can satisfy a search without bringing a reader to the source. That possibility matters here; it does not establish a traffic trend for every publisher. To know what is happening on a particular site, I would separate human visits, crawler requests, referrals, and completed actions. The traffic still comes. The reader behind it arrives less often. That's what makes the optimization instinct so counterproductive. The natural response to declining reach is to optimize harder for the first filter: more SEO, sharper hooks, better headlines. But if the bottleneck has shifted to the second filter, that optimization is solving for the wrong machine. You're getting better at being surfaced by something that routes you to something else that decides you're not worth reading directly. Section 03 What the Second Filter Reads A summary can carry the main claim while losing the sequence of examples that made it convincing. That matters when the point depends on how a reader reaches a conclusion, not just on the conclusion itself. What doesn't compress: vibe, accumulation, the texture of thinking rather than content. The movement from question to observation to something you didn't see coming. That movement is what produces curiosity in a reader, the sense that there's more to find, that the person writing knows something you haven't gotten to yet. The agent reads it, extracts the conclusion, passes along something technically accurate and entirely flat. The essay becomes a bullet point. The argument becomes a sentence. The curiosity doesn't make it through. If you optimize for both filters at once, you end up writing something compressible and positionally consistent. That's a different kind of writing than the kind worth doing. The filter doesn't just change what gets read. It changes what gets built, if you let it. Section 04 Digging with the Wrong Tool The optimization instinct is hard to kill because it used to work, and because the feedback loop that would tell you it stopped working is broken. A total request count does not tell you how many people read a piece. Search impressions and visits answer different questions, and crawler traffic needs separate analysis. The metrics can keep rewarding changes that do not bring more readers to the original piece. Check the version of the work that actually reaches the reader. Measurement is catching up. Google announced dedicated generative AI performance reports in June 2026 . Those reports help identify exposure; they still do not tell me whether a reader understood the argument. The production side compounds this. The content being published is increasingly agentic itself, as argued in the previous essay in this series. An agent creates the piece. Another distributes it. A third, on the reader's side, summarizes it for a human who may or may not have asked for it. At some point in that chain, the question of what any of it means to a person becomes genuinely hard to locate. A production chain instructed to chase SEO checklists and engagement hooks may reproduce those priorities at every step. That is a risk in how the workflow is configured, not proof of what every model was trained to reward. Google’s own guidance says there is no special writing style required for its generative search features. Section 05 The Thing the Filter Can't Flatten There's a version of this that ends in paralysis: if the filters flatten everything, why write anything? But that logic only holds if surviving the filters is the point. The reach model made that feel obvious: you write to be found, being found means a human read you, optimize to be found. Distribution and readership were treated as the same thing. They weren't, even before agents. The second filter just made the gap between them impossible to ignore. What the filter can't flatten is the reason someone seeks the original. A summary can carry a claim. It can't carry the judgment that the person who made the claim is worth trusting. That trust, the sense that a particular voice has a particular relationship to a domain over time, doesn't compress. It accumulates in the person, not in the agent. On the structural shift from reach to indexing, and on the synthesis-without-citation problem: "The Last Human Impression" (diegodella.ar, 2026). "The agent may draw on your perspective to form its answer, and the human who receives that answer never knows you exist. There is no traffic. No referral. The economic model for being synthesized rather than cited is still genuinely unresolved." ✦ ❧ ✦ I want to write work that gives someone a reason to seek the original. diegodella.ar · Buenos Aires, 2026 Share After You Post · Reading Path 01 The Empty Room 02 The Proxy Self 03 Writing for the Filter 04 The Trust Collapse 05 Origin Gravity The Proxy Self The Trust Collapse D DIEGO Diego Dell'Agostino · Media, Product & AI · Argentina Work Writing AI & Media About Speaking Media kit Developers Contact Privacy The idea Reading paths
